The Italian Game (ECO codes C50 to C59) starts with three natural moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Animated sequence of the Italian Game moves 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Each move follows a classical principle: the pawn claims the center, the knight develops while attacking e5, and the bishop aims at f7, the one square only Black's king defends. Fast development, king safety, pressure on f7. That is the whole idea. Why it is called the Italian Game The opening carries the name of the Italian masters who shaped it in the 16th and 17th centuries, above all Gioachino Greco, whose recorded games spread the ideas across Europe long before modern theory existed ( Wikipedia , no-follow). The label stuck because those players documented the bishop-on-c4 attacking plan first. The main idea in one sentence White wants to develop every piece toward Black's king, castle short, and build pressure on f7 before Black finishes coordinating. Nothing here is tricky. The Italian rewards understanding of a plan rather than memory of a computer line, which is exactly why it has survived five centuries of analysis. The first five moves, explained Most Italian games reach the same tabiya. This table walks through the standard build-up and the point of each move. Move White Point 1 e4 Claim the center, open lines for bishop and queen 2 Nf3 Develop with a threat against e5 3 Bc4 Aim the bishop at f7 4 c3 Prepare the d4 central break 5 d3 Support e4, open the c1 bishop, keep it solid After 3...Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3 you have reached the Giuoco Pianissimo, today's most common Italian structure. Both sides are developed, nothing is committed, and the real game is about to begin. Why the Italian Game suits improving players Three reasons make the Italian the best first opening for most players: The plans are logical. Develop, castle, fight for the center. You learn ideas, not memorized computer lines. It is flexible. Steer toward quiet maneuvering or sharp attacks depending on your mood. Theory stays manageable. Compared to the Ruy Lopez or the Sicilian, a handful of key ideas covers most games. If you are still choosing your repertoire, see our overview of the best chess openings for White . The three main variations Black's third move decides which Italian you get. This table gives the map, and each branch is explained below. Variation Black plays Character Best for Giuoco Piano 3...Bc5 Slow, strategic Learning classical plans Evans Gambit 3...Bc5 4.b4 Sharp, sacrificial Attackers Two Knights Defense 3...Nf6 Tactical chaos Fearless calculators Giuoco Piano: the quiet main line Giuoco Piano position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 Giuoco Piano means "quiet game" in Italian. After 3...Bc5 both bishops eye the enemy f-pawns, and play usually continues 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3, the Giuoco Pianissimo. White builds slowly with c3 and d3 before committing to a plan. Why modern grandmasters love it The slow structure keeps every piece on the board and rewards whoever understands the position better. That is why it dominates elite chess today: Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, and Wesley So all trust it in top events, as the master database on the Lichess opening explorer (no-follow) confirms. If world champions choose it over sharper systems, the ideas are sound rather than fashionable. Evans Gambit: the romantic attack Evans Gambit position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 The Evans Gambit offers the b-pawn to gain time: after 4...Bxb4 5.c3 the bishop must move again while White builds a broad center with d4. It was the 19th century's favorite weapon and still scores heavily in club chess. The theory of the Evans Gambit White trades one pawn for two tempi and open lines toward f7. The main line 5...Ba5 6.d4 exd4 7.O-O gives fast development for the pawn. One imprecise defensive move often ends the game. If Black declines with 4...Bb6, White simply gains queenside space for free and keeps a comfortable position. Two Knights Defense: inviting the storm Two Knights Defense position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 With 3...Nf6 Black counterattacks e4 instead of developing quietly. The critical answer 4.Ng5 attacks f7 immediately and leads to the famous Fried Liver complex after 4...d5 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Nxf7. The Fried Liver Attack Fried Liver Attack position after 6.Nxf7 Kxf7, White's bishop bearing down on the exposed king After 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 White sacrifices the knight to drag the black king into the open, then plays 7.Qf3+ and 8.Nc3 hunting the pinned knight on d5. It is one of the sharpest lines a beginner will ever meet. Prefer calm? Answer 3...Nf6 with 4.d3 and transpose to Pianissimo structures instead. Your five-step game plan You do not need twenty moves of theory. This plan covers most club games: Play 1.e4, 2.Nf3 and 3.Bc4 in that order. Castle short early, usually within the first six moves. Support the center with c3 and d3 (or d4 when tactics allow). Reroute the queenside knight: Nbd2, then Nf1 and Ng3 toward the kingside. Start your attack only when every piece has a job. Typical middlegame plans Openings are only useful if you know what comes next. These three plans decide most Italian middlegames. The d3-d4 break After the quiet c3 and d3 setup, the thematic pawn break is d4 at the right moment. Prepare it with Re1 and h3 first. Played too early, it opens the position for Black's pieces; timed well, it wins the center outright and hands White a lasting space edge. The kingside knight tour The queenside knight has a famous journey: Nbd2, Nf1, then Ng3 or Ne3. From g3 it eyes the f5 outpost; from e3 it supports d5. This slow regrouping is the heart of Pianissimo play, and most opponents below 1800 never see the attack coming. Meeting the ...Na5 bishop hunt When Black plays ...Na5 to trade your c4 bishop, you choose: retreat with Bb3 and meet ...Nxb3 with axb3, opening the a-file for your rook, or drop back to c2 keeping the bishop for a later kingside attack. Decide before it happens, not after. Common mistakes to avoid Grabbing f7 too early. Bxf7+ on move four trades your best bishop for a pawn and hands Black's king a safe home in most lines. Blocking the c-pawn. Nc3 before c3 removes your best central lever in Giuoco Piano structures. Ignoring ...Na5. Black often hunts the c4 bishop. Decide in advance: retreat to b3, or allow the trade and take the open file. Attacking with undeveloped pieces. A queen raid before castling usually loses time and the initiative. Italian Game vs Ruy Lopez Both openings start 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6, then split on move three. The choice shapes how much you study. Italian Game (3.Bc4) Ruy Lopez (3.Bb5) Pressure Direct, on f7 Long-term, on the center Theory load Manageable Heavy Best for Most improving players Ambitious theory students Neither is objectively stronger. The Ruy Lopez creates more durable pressure but demands far more memorization; the Italian reaches equally healthy positions with a fraction of the theory. It follows every classical opening principle, the ideas transfer to other openings, and you can play it for years without hitting a theoretical wall. Many coaches make it the first opening they teach, precisely because it teaches real chess instead of memorized traps. Why is it called the Italian Game? It is named after the Italian masters of the 16th and 17th centuries who first analyzed the bishop-to-c4 attack, most famously Gioachino Greco. Their recorded games carried the opening across Europe, and the name has stuck for roughly five hundred years. What are the first five moves of the Italian Game? The standard sequence is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3, reaching the Giuoco Pianissimo. Both sides develop naturally and prepare to castle before the middlegame fight begins. Move orders vary, but this is the backbone most games follow. What does Giuoco Piano mean? Giuoco Piano is Italian for "quiet game". It describes the slow, strategic character of the 3...Bc5 main line, where both sides build up carefully before any real conflict. The even quieter modern treatment with c3 and d3 is called the Giuoco Pianissimo, or "very quiet game". Which grandmasters play the Italian Game? At the top level Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, and many others use the Giuoco Pianissimo regularly. Its return to elite chess in the 2010s proved that a low-theory classical opening can still pose real problems at the highest level. What is the theory of the Evans Gambit? White plays 4.b4, offering a pawn to deflect Black's bishop and gain the tempi for a big center with c3 and d4. In return White accepts a small material deficit for a fast, attacking initiative aimed at f7. It rewards accurate attacking play and punishes passive defense. How long does it take to learn the Italian Game? You can play your first Italian tonight: three moves and a plan is genuinely enough to start. Expect the main Giuoco Piano ideas to feel natural after about twenty games, and the Evans Gambit and Two Knights lines to settle in over a couple of months of casual play. Mainline theory, Austrian Attack and classical systems In the Austrian Attack, White plays f4 early, aiming for a powerful pawn center. Black must react accurately, often with c5 or e5, to avoid being squeezed. Piece placement is critical, and Black needs to know where to put the knights and queen to increase pressure on d4 and e4. In classical systems, White develops more quietly with Nf3 and Be2. Black can respond with c5 and Bg4 or with a quick e5. These positions are slightly less sharp but require a good sense of timing to choose the right pawn break. Because the Pirc allows White many different setups, training your preferred lines in advance will save you a lot of time at the board. Tactical motifs and common errors in the Pirc Tactics in the Pirc often involve undermining White's center. Moves like c5, e5 or even c6 can open lines for the fianchettoed bishop and rooks. Well timed captures on d4 or e4 can reveal tactical shots against an exposed king or loose piece. A common mistake for Black is to delay counterplay for too long. If White is allowed to push e5 and f5 without challenge, the kingside attack can become overwhelming. On the other hand, careless pawn breaks can also backfire if Black's pieces are not ready. Training positions where the center is about to open will help you recognize when tactical resources favour you and when you should reinforce your defences first. Strategic themes and typical middlegames In many Pirc middlegames, Black plays for counterplay on the queenside while White attacks on the kingside. Traditional chess wisdom holds that it is imperative to fight for the center in the opening. This is why beginners are usually advised to start their games by advancing their central pawns. I.e. e4 or d4 for White, and e5 or d5 for Black. With these central pawn advances, the player stakes a claim in the center of the board. They prepare to rapidly develop the rest of their pieces. The Pirc Defense successfully departs from this wisdom. Part of becoming a stronger chess player is knowing when (and how) to break these opening fundamentals! Related : How To Get Better At Chess The Center Trap In the Pirc Defense, Black allows White to gain an “ideal” pawn center with pawns on both e4 and d4 . The reason that Black is willing to concede the center to White is simple. He intends to launch a devastating counter attack later. Instead of occupying the center immediately with pawns, Black will look to exert pressure from the flanks. The Pirc Defense is characterized by Black playing d6 and Nf6 , along with a kingside fianchetto via g6 and Bg7 . Black will most commonly castle kingside next. Would-be Pirc Defense players should know that they cannot allow White to maintain their dominance in the center forever. Black must eventually look to make a central pawn thrust of their own. Either e5 or c5 are thematic moves in the early middlegame for Black to challenge White’s center. Black develops compactly behind the g7-fianchetto, keeps the structure elastic, and picks the moment to strike with …c5 or …e5. It is the King’s Indian philosophy transplanted against 1.e4. The Pirc rewards players who prefer middlegame judgement to forcing theory: there is no single critical line to memorise, but every system demands the right counter. It has served counterattackers from Botvinnik’s era to modern grandmasters as a way to unbalance the game from move one. Key plans & ideas Respect the g7-bishop: it is Black’s best piece — open its diagonal with …c5 or …exd4 rather than burying it behind a fixed …e5. Match the counter to White’s system: …c5 against the Austrian, …e5 against classical setups, fast queenside pawns against the 150 Attack. Use the elastic structure: …c6 and …b5, or …a6 and …b5, gain queenside space and ask White’s centre to justify itself. Don’t rush castling against attacking setups: when White aims Be3, Qd2 and Bh6, a delayed …O-O (or none at all) defuses the standard mating plan. Trade at the right time: exchanges on d4 or e5 convert White’s space into overextension — the Pirc wins its games in the second wave. What it demands is accuracy against White’s sharpest tries, above all the Austrian Attack and the 150 Attack: play them casually and the attack arrives first. What is the difference between the Pirc and the King’s Indian Defense? The opponent’s centre. The KID faces c4 plus d4 and fights a queenside-versus-kingside race; the Pirc faces e4 plus d4, where White has faster attacking schemes but a less stable centre. The ideas rhyme — the move orders and danger zones differ. Pirc or Modern Defense — what separates them? The knight. The Pirc commits …Nf6 early, hitting e4 but giving White a target for e5 advances; the Modern delays it, keeping maximum flexibility at the cost of letting White grab even more space. Many players use both as one repertoire. How should Black meet the Austrian Attack? With the immediate …c5 counter before White finishes the setup. After 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3 c5, the centre comes under fire at its base: lines open while White’s king is still in the middle, turning White’s space into a liability. It is considered a flexible approach for White. By not committing the center, White usually aims to control the center through minor pieces from stable locations. The opening is also known as the Hungarian Opening, and sometimes as the Benko Opening, after grandmaster Pal Benko, who employed 1.g3 regularly at the top level. The term fianchetto itself describes the way the Bishop is developed: the Knight’s pawn advances one square and the Bishop is placed on the long diagonal behind it. In this opening, that means the f1-Bishop travels to g2, where it eyes the a8-h1 diagonal for the rest of the game. It was played by many of the top players over time. Its debut at the elite level dates back to the 1800s. Many grandmasters nowadays use it for fast time controls due to its practical usage. Main Ideas In this opening, White usually aims to create a fianchetto square for the f1-Bishop and place the g1-Knight at f3 . d3- and e4-pawn pushes are typical to claim the center later on. By not playing the orthodox e4- or d4- moves , White seeks to strike back and utilize its g2-Bishop . The pawn structure in this move order is often favorable for White since there are no certain weaknesses if the game proceeds correctly. Black usually equalizes quickly; however, the lack of a plan may lead them to make significant positional mistakes. Theoretical Lines in King’s Fianchetto Opening The 1..d5 line usually gives the center to Black, whereas White places their pieces strategically to undermine them and create weaknesses in the opponent’s position. The 2…c6 line often allows Black’s light square Bishop out and gives them a Slav-type structure. White usually plays a similar set-up as the other variations. These games are generally closed in terms of pawn structure. The 3…Bg4 line, in general, leads positions where White aims to open up the ‘a8-h1’ diagonal to exploit the b7-pawn’s vulnerability. Black often seeks to put pressure on the f3-Knight. 1…Nf6 is a flexible approach where the game can lead to both strategic and tactical battles, depending on the continuation. 1…d5 variation It starts with 1…d5 . It is the most common reply to 1.g3 at amateur and master levels. By going with the d-pawn forward, Black seeks to claim the center. White usually fianchettos the f1-Bishop into g2 and places the Knight on f3 in different move orders. White usually plays d3 and e4 moves to activate the scope of the g2-Bishop. If Black tries to lock the center by pushing the pawns, White can launch an attack in the Kingside, similar to the King’s Indian Attack , where the f-pawn can be moved forward, and the minor pieces can be stacked up on the Kingside to hunt the rival King. Where the King’s Fianchetto Opening Transposes One of the strongest practical features of 1.g3 is that it rarely stays a pure “system” for long. Because White delays committing the center, the same kingside fianchetto can flow into several well-known structures, often catching Black in a middlegame they do not normally play. If White follows up with c4 and d4, the game frequently transposes into a Catalan-type structure, where the g2-Bishop bears down on Black’s d5-pawn and White presses on the queenside. If White instead chooses d3 and e4 with the Knight heading to e2, the position takes on the character of a King’s Indian Attack, where the f-pawn advance and a kingside piece build-up become the main plan against the enemy King. Against an early …c5 by Black, White can steer the game toward a Closed Sicilian set-up with d3, e4, Nc3 and Nge2, again with f4-f5 as the thematic kingside break. A c4-based approach without an early d4, on the other hand, simply becomes an English Opening with colors and move order rearranged. For White, the practical value is the same in every case: the opponent is invited onto ground that White has prepared and Black may not have. Pros and Cons Pros Cons White can undermine the opponent’s pawn structure and create weak pawns for the endgame if the rival overextends. It usually requires understanding pawn structures and positional chess to create a plan. Black cannot prove an advantage easily. It is not simple to generate the King’s Fianchetto Opening counter. White often gives up the center. Endgames often favor White due to the solid pawn structure. White may feel suffocated in space in certain lines. Players with better strategy can prove their chess ability compared to low-level players without getting into tactical complications. Black usually equalizes easily. How to Counter the King’s Fianchetto Opening Because White gives up the immediate fight for the center, the most reliable response for Black is to take that space directly. The classical antidote is to build a broad pawn center: 1…d5 followed by …e5, supported by …Nf6 and …Nc6. With pawns on d5 and e5 and pieces developed naturally, Black removes much of White’s counterattacking potential before it appears. A few practical guidelines make the King’s Fianchetto Opening far less dangerous for the second player. Black should develop with a clear plan rather than mirroring White passively, since a planless set-up is exactly what allows White’s strategy to take over. The light-squared Bishop should not be traded for the f3-Knight without good reason, as that hands White’s g2-Bishop extra strength on the long diagonal. Finally, Black must keep an eye on the b7-pawn and the a8-h1 diagonal, since most of White’s pressure in these lines is generated there. When Black occupies the center confidently and develops with purpose, equality comes naturally, and it is genuinely difficult for White to prove any opening advantage. Anish Giri vs. Leinier Dominguez Perez, 2023 You must activate JavaScript to enhance chess game visualization. FAQ’s What is a fianchetto in chess? A fianchetto is a way of developing a Bishop onto a long diagonal: you advance the Knight’s pawn one square (g3 or b3 for White) and place the Bishop behind it on g2 or b2. This gives the Bishop long-range control across the board. What is the best response to the King’s Fianchetto Opening? The most reliable reply for Black is to occupy the center with pawns on d5 and e5, supported by …Nf6 and …Nc6. Developing with a clear plan, rather than copying White, is the simplest way to neutralize 1.g3. Is the King’s Fianchetto the same as the Benko Opening? Yes. The opening starting with 1.g3 goes by several names, the King’s Fianchetto Opening, the Hungarian Opening, and the Benko Opening, but they all describe the same first move. Is King’s Fianchetto a Good Opening? The King’s Fianchetto is considered a solid and flexible opening. It allows for a strong bishop placement and can lead to a robust pawn structure. However, its effectiveness depends on the player’s style and the opponent’s response. Is the Hungarian Opening Good for Beginners? The Hungarian Opening can be a good choice for beginners. It is less aggressive and more about controlling the center and positioning, which can be beneficial for players still learning the game’s nuances. This can happen intentionally or unintentionally, and it often requires players to be adaptable and familiar with various openings and positions.
